For Immediate Release: 
 September 28, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Emcitate (tiratricol) tablets for oral suspension to treat peripheral thyrotoxicosis (excess thyroid hormone levels in the blood that causes symptoms, such as rapid heart rate, increased blood pressure and adverse effects on metabolism) in patients with MCT8 deficiency, also known as Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome. Emcitate is the first therapy approved by the FDA to treat symptoms of this very rare, devastating genetic disease. This approval reflects the FDA’s dedication to patients with rare genetic diseases, many of whom have serious unmet medical needs.
 “Until now, patients living with MCT8 deficiency and their families had no FDA-approved treatment option,” said Marina Zemskova, M.D., Deputy Director of the Division of General Endocrinology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Emcitate’s approval reflects the FDA’s deep commitment to patients with rare conditions who are in need of meaningful treatment options.”
 MCT8 deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that primarily affects males. The condition is caused by a faulty gene that provides instructions for making the MCT8 transporter, a critical protein responsible for carrying thyroid hormone into the brain. Because thyroid hormone cannot cross the blood-brain barrier without the MCT8 transporter, the brain receives too little of this hormone, while excessive levels of the hormone build up in the bloodstream. Many patients with MCT8 deficiency experience a range of debilitating effects, including the inability to walk or sit independently, absent or severely limited speech, intellectual disability, feeding difficulties and chronic stress on the heart and metabolism.
 “The challenge in treating MCT8 deficiency has always been that the protein needed to deliver thyroid hormone into cells is the one that isn’t working,” said Hylton V. Joffe, M.D., MMSc, Director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This drug sidesteps that problem, as its active ingredient, tiratricol, can enter cells on its own without relying on the broken transporter, leading to a decrease in the elevated blood thyroid hormone levels.”
 The effectiveness of Emcitate was evaluated in two clinical studies in patients ranging in age from infants to adults, including an international, multi-center, randomized, placebo-controlled trial ( NCT05579327 ) and a longer-term open-label study. Across both studies, patients treated with Emcitate had reductions in excess thyroid hormone levels in the bloodstream and improvements in cardiovascular and metabolic symptoms impacted by thyroid levels, such as systolic blood pressure and heart rate.
 Emcitate is taken once daily as a liquid suspension, either by mouth or through a feeding tube for patients who have difficulty swallowing, making it accessible for patients with a wide range of abilities. The most common side effects were diarrhea, vomiting, rash and excessive sweating. Patients taking another thyroid medication should talk to their healthcare provider before starting Emcitate, as the two should not be used together.
 Emcitate was granted Orphan Drug , Rare Pediatric Disease , Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review . The approval of Emcitate was granted to Egetis Therapeutics US Inc.

For Immediate Release: 
 September 29, 2026 
 The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida and the Criminal Division of the U.S. Department of Justice today announced federal charges against Swapnadip Roy, 33, and Vicky Ramancha, 37, both Indian nationals. The two individuals have been charged with conspiracy and smuggling related to an alleged transnational counterfeit prescription drug distribution scheme. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Office of Criminal Investigations assisted with this investigation.
 “Infiltrating the American drug supply with counterfeit products isn’t just a crime — it’s also a direct threat to public health and patient safety,” said Acting FDA Commissioner of Food and Drugs, Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “The FDA will continue to trace illicit networks wherever they lead, across borders and through complex supply chains, to ensure that anyone who seeks to profit off counterfeit medicines face accountability — all in our mission to keep Americans safe.”
 According to court documents, between July 2023 and April 2024, Roy and Ramancha allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The counterfeit Ozempic allegedly distributed by Roy, Ramancha, and their co-conspirators included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers, including pharmacies and patients, into believing they were receiving authentic, manufacturer-authorized Ozempic. The indictment alleges that Roy, Ramancha, and their co-conspirators sold the counterfeit Ozempic to other co-conspirators and distributors in the U.S. at deeply discounted prices.
 The FDA issued public safety alerts starting in December 2023 to warn consumers, pharmacies, and healthcare providers about counterfeit Ozempic products. Notably, court documents allege that Roy, Ramancha, and their co-conspirators continued distributing counterfeit Ozempic even after FDA’s December 2023 seizure and public warning.
 The agency takes reports of possible counterfeit medicines seriously and works closely with other federal agencies and the private sector to help protect the nation’s drug supply. Entities, including online sellers, selling counterfeit and/or tampered medicines should be reported to the FDA. Suspected counterfeit products may be reported by going to Report a problem to the FDA . 
 An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

For Immediate Release: 
 September 30, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced a broad, nationwide recruitment effort to expand the range of qualified voices and perspectives on its advisory committees— the independent bodies that inform some of the most consequential decisions in American public health. As part of an effort to broaden and strengthen participation on its advisory committees, the FDA is publishing two Federal Register notices: one seeking qualified scientific, technical, and professional voting members across all committees with current or anticipated vacancies, and a companion notice seeking consumer representatives to ensure the public’s voice is at the table. 
 “FDA advisory committees bring together leading scientific minds to engage with the most difficult questions in public health. We are actively inviting people from across the country who are on the forefront of their fields — clinicians, researchers, and community voices who can bring the latest science, real-world experience, and fresh perspectives to the FDA’s deliberations,” said Acting FDA Commissioner of Food and Drugs, Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “These panels provide independent expertise and rigorous scrutiny as the FDA navigates complex and rapidly evolving areas of science. The Trump Administration is deeply committed to strengthening the partnership between the FDA and the nation’s brightest minds. 
 Advisory committees are a cornerstone of the FDA’s science-based, transparent regulatory process. These committees and panels bring together scientific experts such as physicians, researchers, biostatisticians, along with patient advocates and consumer representatives to evaluate the evidence on drugs, vaccines, biologics, medical devices, and other FDA-regulated products — providing independent recommendations that help the FDA make well-informed decisions on behalf of the American public.
 The FDA is recruiting qualified candidates for vacancies spanning multiple scientific domains — from oncology and cardiovascular medicine to neurology, genetics, and medical devices. Interested candidates — whether applying as scientific experts or as consumer representatives — are encouraged to begin the process through the centralized FDA Advisory Committee Membership Nomination application portal .
 Nominees for scientific and technical voting member positions must demonstrate subject-matter expertise relevant to one or more FDA advisory committees, the ability to interpret complex scientific and technical information, an understanding of the public health significance of issues before the committee, and the capacity to provide objective, independent advice. Nominees for consumer representative positions should have demonstrated affiliation with or active participation in consumer or community-based organizations, and the ability to analyze technical data, discuss benefits and risks, and evaluate product safety and efficacy from a public perspective.
 The FDA will consider nominations for current and anticipated near-term vacancies and will accept nominations on a continuing basis. To receive first consideration for current and near-term vacancies, nominations for consumer representative positions should be submitted no later than November 15, 2026, and nominations for scientific, technical, professional, and other voting-member positions should be submitted no later than November 30, 2026. Nominations received after these dates will be considered as later vacancies arise. Self-nominations are accepted. Members are invited to serve for terms of up to four years.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 01, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve, a surgically implanted pulmonary heart valve for pediatric patients with congenital pulmonary valve disease. This innovative device may reduce the need for repeat open-heart surgeries in children with heart defects, reflecting the Trump Administration’s commitment to bringing breakthrough medical technologies to market as quickly and safely as possible.
 The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve is the first heart valve designed to be expanded after surgery to keep pace with a child’s growth, and the first valve approved in the U.S. to use polymeric material rather than animal-derived tissue for its inner flaps (called leaflets).
 “For far too long, children with congenital heart defects who need pulmonary valve replacement have had very limited surgical options, and those options have historically required multiple open-heart surgeries as children grow,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Today’s landmark approval is a historic turning point and reflects the Trump Administration and the FDA’s commitment to help bring innovative, life-changing devices to the patients who need them most.”
 Congenital heart defects are among the most common types of birth defects in the United States, affecting about 1 in every 100 births. Among these conditions are pulmonary valve abnormalities — including pulmonary valve stenosis, in which the valve is narrowed, and pulmonary valve atresia, in which the valve fails to form normally — both of which restrict blood flow from the heart to the lungs. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , pulmonary valve atresia and stenosis together affect around 4,200 babies in the United States each year.
 While treatment can improve blood flow and help repair these congenital defects, some children may be left with significant pulmonary regurgitation, or leakage of blood back through the pulmonary valve. Over time, this can weaken or enlarge the right ventricle and create a need for pulmonary valve replacement as the child grows.
 “For children born with congenital heart disease, valve replacement timing has always been a difficult decision — wait too long and you risk harm to the child, but intervene too early and they may need multiple open-heart surgeries as they grow,” said Michelle Tarver, M.D., Ph.D., director of the FDA’s Center for Devices and Radiological Health . “The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve gives doctors the option of far fewer trips to the operating room, which may result in better quality of life for these children and their families.”
 The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve can be initially implanted as small as approximately 13 millimeters in diameter — the right size for a toddler or preschool-aged child — and later widened using a small inflatable tube (balloon catheter) as the child grows, eventually reaching up to 22 millimeters, which is comparable to an adult-sized pulmonary valve.
 In addition, the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve uses polymeric material for its leaflets — the flaps inside the valve that open and close to control blood flow. Traditional valves use tissue derived from animals, which tends to harden and break down faster in children, often requiring earlier repeat surgery. One-year follow-up data suggest the Autus valve’s synthetic leaflets hold up well over time. This is the first time the FDA has approved a valve that uses polymeric leaflet material for any indication.
 The FDA’s approval is based on data from a clinical study, which enrolled 62 pediatric patients across 12 U.S. sites. At the six-month follow-up, the first 60 patients demonstrated acceptable hemodynamic performance, meaning blood flow through the right side of the heart was within acceptable limits, and there was no more than mild leakage back through the valve. All patients in the study had a successful procedure, with no deaths, blood clots requiring additional treatment, strokes or other clot-related complications. Three patients experienced a fracture in the valve frame and two patients had reduced movement of one of the valve leaflets (the flaps that open and close), but none of these events resulted in symptoms for the patients. Additionally, valve performance began deteriorating in two patients who started to outgrow it. Both patients had their valves successfully expanded without an invasive surgical procedure, but the experience is limited. Longer-term studies are being conducted to better understand these risks, and to collect more data to show that expansion can maintain a functional valve that may lead to fewer surgical procedures for patients.
 The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve is the first pediatric approval to come out of the FDA’s Total Product Life Cycle Advisory Program (TAP) , a voluntary program for device developers intended to spur more rapid development of high-quality, safe, effective and innovative medical devices for all patients. The FDA previously granted the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve Breakthrough Device designation , which is meant to expedite the development and review of devices that provide for more effective treatment or diagnosis of life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating diseases or conditions.
 The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve was approved through the premarket approval pathway, the FDA’s most stringent type of medical device marketing application. The pathway is used for certain Class III devices, which generally pose the greatest risk. Before approving a device, the FDA reviews scientific evidence, including nonclinical and clinical data, to determine whether there is reasonable assurance that the device is safe and effective for its intended use and whether the benefits outweigh the known risks.
 Edwards Lifesciences received approval for the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve, developed by Autus Valve Technologies Inc.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 05, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced a request for information (RFI) describing approaches the agency is considering for the design of early-phase clinical trials of ibogaine drug products and seeking public input on those approaches. The RFI seeks comments, data, and information on specific protocol elements relevant to ibogaine drug development, including dose selection and escalation, care setting, safety monitoring, eligibility criteria, stopping rules and safety oversight. This RFI marks the latest FDA action to advance President Trump’s April 2026 executive order on Accelerating Medical Treatments for Serious Mental Illness , which directed agencies to accelerate research into psychedelic medicine.
 “Patients facing serious conditions that have not responded to existing treatments deserve rigorous scientific investigation of promising new approaches,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “With ibogaine, there are important scientific questions as well as serious safety concerns. We are seeking high-quality data and input that can help inform clinical research while putting patient safety first.”
 The FDA is seeking comments, data and information in four primary areas:
 General study design , including appropriate patient populations;
 Dose selection and escalation , including the proposed use of small, sequential dose-ascending groups and a starting dose justified by available data and not exceeding 10 mg/kg;
 Safety considerations , including monitoring for cardiac and neurologic adverse events and other safeguards for clinical trials; and
 Ethical and oversight considerations , including informed consent and appropriate independent safety oversight.
 The FDA recognizes the seriousness of the conditions and unmet needs that patients seeking ibogaine treatments face. The information received through this RFI may help the agency better understand the potential uses, benefits and risks of ibogaine drug products and inform approaches to drug development.
 The FDA has been working across the federal government to support the responsible development of ibogaine drug products through careful evidence-based processes. In July 2026, the FDA issued its finalized guidance for industry, Psychedelic Drugs: Considerations for Clinical Investigations , which provides general considerations for sponsors developing psychedelic drugs. The FDA has also allowed an early-phase clinical study of noribogaine hydrochloride , a derivative of ibogaine, to proceed under an Investigational New Drug application as a potential treatment for alcohol use disorder.
 As part of the whole-of-government approach to advance psychedelic drug development, HHS, through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) , is funding a program to collect safety and efficacy data through early-phase clinical trials, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) is funding research on ibogaine for the potential treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD). Based on available data and the seriousness of the conditions, HHS is prioritizing two initial populations for federally supported research: adults with OUD and adults with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
 The public will have 45 days following publication in the Federal Register to submit comments, data or information to the docket. Stakeholders are encouraged to submit comments electronically at regulations.gov by searching for Docket No. FDA-2026-N-10429 . Written/paper submissions may also be sent to: Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.
 The comment period closes Friday, November 20, 2026. Late comments will not be considered.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 14, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today expanded the approved use of Anktiva (nogapendekin alfa inbakicept-pmln), given with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), to include adults with high-grade papillary-only bladder cancer that has not spread into the bladder muscle and has not responded to BCG treatment. Anktiva is the first FDA-approved treatment specifically for patients with BCG-unresponsive, high-grade papillary-only disease. 
 The approval marks a new FDA approach to evaluating treatments for BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). The agency based its decision on evidence supporting an earlier approval of Anktiva for adults with another form of NMIBC, carcinoma in situ (CIS), with or without papillary tumors, and scientific similarities between CIS and high-grade papillary-only disease.
 “We listen to patients, clinicians, and researchers, and we act when the science supports a new approach,” said R. Angelo de Claro, M.D., Director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “For Anktiva, our review of the similarities between these cancers allowed us to build on the results in patients with CIS and expand treatment options for people with high-grade papillary tumors alone. This approach may also help guide the development of future treatments.”
 NMIBC is bladder cancer that has not grown into the bladder’s muscle layer and can include CIS and papillary tumors. CIS forms flat patches along the bladder’s lining, while papillary tumors grow from the lining into the bladder as small, finger-like projections. CIS is always high-grade, while papillary tumors can be low-grade or high-grade. High-grade cancers are more likely to grow and spread than low-grade cancers. 
 Treatment for high-risk NMIBC often starts with BCG, which activates the immune system inside the bladder to fight cancer. Sometimes, however, the cancer persists or returns. Adding Anktiva gives the immune system another way to fight the cancer, and the combination can help some people whose cancer was not controlled by BCG alone.
 Anktiva’s CIS approval was supported by a trial ( NCT03022825 ) that evaluated the treatment’s effectiveness in 77 adults, some of whom also had papillary tumors. Sixty-two percent achieved a complete response, meaning no high-grade cancer was detected during follow-up assessments, and of those, 58% maintained that response for at least 12 months and 40% for at least 24 months.
 For today’s expanded approval, the FDA considered these results alongside clinical and laboratory evidence showing that CIS and high-grade papillary tumors share important features. They often occur together, can be difficult to distinguish under a microscope and carry a high risk of returning or progressing when BCG treatment no longer works. These similarities supported applying the evidence of Anktiva’s effectiveness in people with CIS to those with high-grade papillary-only disease.
 To help developers apply this approach, the FDA is working toward finalizing its draft guidance, “ Bacillus Calmette-Guérin-Unresponsive Nonmuscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: Developing Drugs and Biological Products for Treatment .” The guidance is intended to include discussion of using evidence from studies in patients with CIS to support approval of treatments for BCG-unresponsive, high-grade papillary-only NMIBC. 
 Anktiva is given with BCG directly into the bladder through a catheter. It is given once a week for six weeks, with additional treatment based on how the cancer responds. Treatment may continue for up to 37 months. It should be stopped if the cancer persists after a second six-week course, returns or progresses, or side effects become unacceptable.
 The most common side effects and laboratory abnormalities included painful or frequent urination, an urgent need to urinate, blood in the urine, urinary tract infections, muscle or joint pain, chills, fever, and increased blood levels of creatinine and potassium. Anktiva’s prescribing information warns that delaying surgery to remove all or part of the bladder can allow the cancer to spread to other parts of the body, which can be fatal. 
 The approval was granted to Altor BioScience, LLC.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 14, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), today announced the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to reimagine the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. As outlined in a new white paper , the Initiative will develop an optimized, fit-for-purpose framework that reflects the realities of rare disease drug development by considering the nuances of each disease, patient needs, product type and the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations.
 To solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative from patients and disease advocates, industry, and others, the FDA will host an October 28 meeting at the FDA’s White Oak campus. The meeting will be facilitated by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA.
 “Americans with rare diseases cannot afford a regulatory system that treats every condition the same,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump, FDA is rethinking rare disease drug development by putting patients at the center and matching regulatory requirements to the realities of small patient populations. We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.” 
 “Patients and families living with rare diseases have few or no approved treatment options, and the burden of uncertainty can extend across every part of their lives,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront — prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them. The FDA will fight hard for patients by building a more consistent, predictable, and innovative approach to rare disease drug development while maintaining the rigorous standards Americans expect from the FDA.”
 The FDA has long used regulatory flexibility and developed targeted programs to support innovation in the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. These efforts have led to meaningful advances for patients and families. Nevertheless, with only 5% or so of rare conditions having an FDA-approved treatment, the FDA agrees with patients, drug developers, and providers that more must be done to speed the development of safe and effective treatments for rare diseases. In developing the framework, the FDA is committed to the following:
 Providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication.
 Embedding the patient’s voice both early, and at clearly defined milestones, in the drug development and review process.
 Further leveraging external expertise to support customization of regulatory review.
 Building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review.
 Applying risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections.
 Championing the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and innovative statistical approaches in rare disease drug development.
 The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.
 “Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards,” said the Hub’s Director, Amy Comstock Rick, J.D. “A bold vision to reimagine the framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.”
 Further opportunities to provide input will follow the public meeting, including sector-specific roundtables, Requests for Information, and internal FDA feedback sessions. This feedback will inform the detailed development of a new framework, which might include potential new or revised guidance, revisions to regulations, staff training, and organizational changes.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 19, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life.
 Patients with locally advanced rectal cancer often receive chemotherapy and radiation prior to surgery, which can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility. Surgery also carries risks of serious, sometimes life-threatening complications, including poor healing and leaks where the bowel is reconnected, and in some patients, permanent colostomy.
 “The FDA is committed to closing the gap between scientific progress and patient access, and that commitment has to show up not just in policy, but in the pace of our work,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “American patients deserve timely access to innovative treatments, and the Trump Administration is making that a reality. Completing this review nearly 4 months ahead of schedule means some patients who might otherwise be preparing for surgery, radiation or chemotherapy may now have a different conversation with their doctor.”
 Today’s approval is for Jemperli used alone in adults with previously untreated stage II or stage III locally advanced rectal cancer. At these stages, the cancer has grown into nearby tissue or reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. To be eligible, patients’ tumors must be mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), as determined by an FDA-authorized test. Published estimates suggest that approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR or MSI-H.
 Both terms describe a defect in the way cancer cells correct errors when copying their DNA. Normally, a built-in repair system catches and fixes these mistakes. When the system does not work properly, errors accumulate and create proteins the immune system can recognize, making these tumors particularly vulnerable to immunotherapy.
 Jemperli works by blocking a signal that cancer cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. Specifically, it targets a protein called PD-1 on immune cells.
 “Standard treatment for rectal cancer has major life-changing effects. For certain types of rectal cancer, this approval represents a groundbreaking option that avoids surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. This represents a significant benefit for patients and their families,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “The FDA is acting on emerging evidence to bring new approaches to patients sooner, while requiring further studies to confirm that these treatments provide lasting benefits.”
 The FDA based its decision on interim results from AZUR-1 ( NCT05723562 ), a phase 2 study evaluating Jemperli alone in 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. In the study, patients received up to nine doses of Jemperli, given every 3 weeks over 6 months. After a median follow-up of more than 2 years — meaning at least half of patients had been monitored for that long — almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Longer follow-up is needed to understand the duration of response and how often the cancer returns.
 An earlier study at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center ( NCT04165772 ) evaluated Jemperli alone in 50 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. None of the patients had detectable signs of cancer after Jemperli treatment, and nearly all patients (93%) maintained that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. Of the 27 patients followed for at least 3 years, only one had their cancer return, and it recurred in the same area.
 Jemperli can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs and tissues. These reactions can be severe or fatal. The most common side effects, reported in at least 15% of patients treated for this type of rectal cancer, were fatigue, rash, diarrhea and itching.
 The FDA granted Priority Review to the application and Breakthrough Therapy designation to Jemperli for the treatment of dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. This action marks the 11th approval of a drug reviewed under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program , which aims to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities. Because this is an accelerated approval based on interim trial results, the sponsor must continue following patients to show these responses create lasting clinical benefit.
 The approval was granted to GSK.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 20, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency.
 “Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.”
 The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users.
 The guidance identifies two categories of companion software:
 Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used.
 Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising.
 “This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.”
 “Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology . “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.”
 This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on.

 Treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause
 Prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis

Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are specifically approved for women with an intact uterus, as the progestogen component is included to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with estrogen use alone.

For Immediate Release: 
 October 20, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. 
 “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.”
 Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body.
 The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. 
 Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements.
 Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. 
 Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. 
 The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review . The approval was granted to GSK plc.

text:
For Immediate Release: 
 October 30, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options.
 “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) . “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.”
 The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit.
 RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. 
 Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11). Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells.
 The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment.
 The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site.
 The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

For Immediate Release: 
 November 02, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically.
 The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement. 
 "Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research . "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety."
 The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies.
 By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence. 
 The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance.

For Immediate Release: 
 November 05, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval to Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. HNSCC is an aggressive, life-threatening disease for which there is a high unmet need for effective therapies.
 Rybrevant Faspro is not indicated as a treatment for patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma that is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). 
 Approval was based on trial results showing that more than double the percentage of patients responded to the drug compared to currently approved therapies. This is the first approval in 10 years of a drug for patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC who had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. 
 “Today’s approval represents a meaningful step forward for patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a disease where treatment options have historically been limited and outcomes remain poor,” said Angelo De Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “This therapy offers patients and their physicians a new option with the potential to make a real difference in people’s lives.”
 The Accelerated Approval Program allows for earlier approval of drugs that treat serious conditions and fill an unmet medical need based on surrogate or intermediate endpoints. In this case, accelerated approval of Rybrevant Faspro was granted based on overall response rate and duration of response. Since it is not yet confirmed whether this will translate into a clinically meaningful benefit in long-term outcomes, the FDA has required confirmatory studies to verify and describe clinical benefit.
 In an open-label, multicenter clinical trial involving 102 patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, Rybrevant Faspro had an overall response rate of 42%, meaning these patients saw their tumor either decrease in size or disappear. Of those patients who had a response, 56% had a response lasting six months or longer. Currently approved therapies are associated with an overall response rate of around 20% or less and poor outcomes.
 The prescribing information for use as a single agent includes warnings and precautions for hypersensitivity and administration-related reactions, interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, dermatologic adverse reactions, ocular toxicity, and harm to an unborn baby. 
 The FDA granted Rybrevant Faspro Breakthrough Therapy designation for this indication. The approval was granted to Janssen Biotech, Inc.

For Immediate Release: 
 November 09, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Sunharbo (asundexian) 50 mg tablets, the first factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a clot that did not originate in the heart) or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a “mini-stroke.” 
 “Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, and survivors are at risk of having another stroke,” said Hylton V. Joffe, M.D., MMSc, Director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Today’s approval represents a meaningful advance for patients and health care providers seeking a new option for secondary stroke prevention.” 
 The effectiveness of Sunharbo was demonstrated in the OCEANIC-STROKE study , a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study that enrolled 12,327 adults. Participants had a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIH Stroke Scale ≤15) or high-risk TIA and were randomly assigned to Sunharbo or placebo within 72 hours of symptom onset. Both groups also received antiplatelet therapy. Sunharbo 50 mg once daily significantly reduced the risk of ischemic stroke by 26% compared to placebo over a median treatment of 14.2 months. 
 The overall rate of major bleeding was similar between the Sunharbo and placebo groups but was increased with Sunharbo in patients older than 75 years and during the first 90 days of treatment. Gastrointestinal bleeding occurred more commonly with Sunharbo compared to placebo. The most frequently reported adverse reaction (occurring in 3% or greater of Sunharbo-treated patients) was diarrhea. 
 Concomitant use with medicines that are combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inducers (such as carbamazepine) is not recommended because these medicines may decrease Sunharbo’s effectiveness. Sunharbo is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Sunharbo should be withheld at least 24 hours before elective surgery or invasive procedures and for at least 24 hours after thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke. Sunharbo is not approved for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. 
 The FDA granted Sunharbo Fast Track and Priority Review designations. The approval was granted to Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals Inc., Whippany, N.J.

BACKGROUND: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. We evaluated this combination as neoadjuvant therapy and investigated its effect on peripheral immunity and the tumour microenvironment.
METHODS: PRIME-HCC is a single-arm, phase 1b trial in adults (aged ≥18 years) with early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A liver function, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1. Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 22 of the first and second cycle) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously on day 1 of the first cycle only) before liver resection. The primary endpoint was safety, assessed by treatment-related delays to surgery and adverse events in the intention-to-treat population. Translational analyses included imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics on paired tumour samples, peripheral immunophenotyping, T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, and longitudinal tumour-agnostic circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) profiling. This trial was registered with EudraCT (2018-000987-27) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03682276); follow-up is currently ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Sept 18, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, of 43 patients assessed for eligibility, 33 patients were enrolled (25 [76%] male and 8 [24%] female; median age 68 years [range 38-80; IQR 63-73]); median follow-up was 25·7 months (95% CI 21·2-30·1). Any-grade adverse events occurred in 31 (94%) of patients, with treatment-related adverse events (trAEs) in 25 (76%) patients. Grade 3 trAEs occurred in three (9%) patients (transaminase elevation, anaemia, and dyspnoea). Serious adverse events were recorded in three (9%) patients, and no grade 4-5 events or treatment-related deaths occurred. 30 (91%) patients underwent surgery, including two (6%) who had immune checkpoint inhibitor-related surgical delays. Objective response rate by RECIST 1.1 was noted in eight (25%; 95% CI 13-42) patients (one complete response and seven partial responses), with 31 (97%; 84-100) patients achieving disease control. The absence of ctDNA after surgery was associated with improved 2-year recurrence-free survival (nine [82%] of 11 patients vs two [29%] of seven; p=0·049), as was at least 50% ctDNA reduction (median not reached [95% CI not reached] vs 20·9 months [95% CI 16·3-25·4]; HR 0·14 [95% CI 0·02-0·91]; p=0·039). Patients with objective responses showed expansion of peripheral PD-1-positive, Ki-67-positive, CD8-positive T cells (T-responding exhausted cells [Tresp]), associated with higher baseline intratumoral progenitor-exhausted T cells (Tpex) and increased Tresp infiltration. Patients whose disease did not respond to treatment exhibited enrichment of terminally exhausted CD8-positive T cells (Tex-term; CD8-positive PD-1-positive TOX-positive cells) and regulatory T cells.
INTERPRETATION: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab is feasible in early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, and later-phase randomised trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of this treatment strategy. Longitudinal ctDNA monitoring could support detection of minimal residual disease and warrants further prospective validation.
FUNDING: Bristol Myers Squibb, Cancer Research UK, Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro, and Foundation for Liver Research.
title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in surgically resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (PRIME-HCC): a prospective, phase 1b, single-arm trial and translational analyses.

BACKGROUND: Functional loss of B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a recognised mechanism of relapse after BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Targeting multiple tumour antigens simultaneously with a single CAR has the potential to mitigate antigen escape and prolong disease responses. Transmembrane activator and CAML interactor (TACI) and BCMA are both highly expressed on most myeloma cells and bind to the same natural ligand-a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL). We designed TriPRIL, a CAR that uses an engineered trimeric form of APRIL, to target both BCMA and TACI. We aimed to establish the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, and recommended phase 2 dose of autologous TriPRIL CAR T cells.
METHODS: In this first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and dose-expansion, phase 1 study, we evaluated TriPRIL in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, MA, USA). Eligible patients had received at least three previous lines of therapy or had triple-class refractory disease. Previous CAR T-cell therapy and bispecific antibody therapy exposure were permitted. Patients received 3 days of lymphodepletion with intravenous cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m 2 ) and intravenous fludarabine (30 mg/m 2 ) daily on days -5, -4, and -3 before intravenous TriPRIL infusion on day 0. In the dose escalation phase, patients received 1·0 × 10 8 or 3·0 × 10 8 TriPRIL CAR T cells to establish the recommended phase 2 dose, which was further evaluated in the dose expansion phase. The primary endpoint was the incidence of study-related adverse events (graded according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5) and dose-limiting toxicities in all patients who received an infusion of TriPRIL CAR T cells, until study completion at 24 months or progressive disease. The data cutoff date was March 24, 2026, when all infused patients had completed at least one assessment of disease response. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05020444), has fully accrued, and is ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Sept 17, 2021, and Jan 27, 2026, 16 patients were enrolled and underwent leukapheresis, with 15 patients subsequently receiving a TriPRIL cell infusion. Ten (67%) of 15 infused patients were female, five (33%)were male, and the median age was 69 years (IQR 65-75). Nine (60%) of 15 infused patients had previously received BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy, and four (27%) had previously received a BCMA-directed or GPRC5D-directed bispecific T-cell engager. Six patients were treated with 1·0 × 10 8 CAR T cells, and nine were treated with 3·0 × 10 8 CAR T cells; there were no dose-limiting toxicities at either dose. The most common adverse events were neutropenia (14 [93%] of 15 patients), nausea (12 [80%]), hypogammaglobulinaemia (eight [53%]), fatigue (seven [47%]), and fever (seven [47%]). Non-haematological adverse events grade 3 or worse occurred in five (33%) patients and all resolved. Cytokine release syndrome (grade 1 or 2 only) occurred in 13 (87%, 95% CI 60-98) infused patients. One (7%, 0-32) patient had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and one (7%, 0-32) had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome; both of these patients had received 3·0 × 10 8 CAR T cells, and both conditions resolved with corticosteroids. Infections occurred in six (40%, 16-68) infused patients, with a grade 3 infection in one patient (7%, 0-32). There were no treatment-related deaths. The recommended phase 2 dose of CAR T cells was set as 3·0 × 10 8 cells.
INTERPRETATION: TriPRIL showed a favourable safety profile and warrants further investigation in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, including those previously treated with BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy. The study findings support further development of this dual-targeted, natural ligand-based CAR T-cell approach.
FUNDING: Mass General Brigham and V Foundation.
title: Natural ligand-based CAR T-cell therapy targeting BCMA and TACI for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (TriPRIL): a non-randomised, phase 1, first-in-human trial.

PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to investigate whether external-beam accelerated partial-breast irradiation (APBI) provides noninferior local control compared with whole-breast irradiation (WBI).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted this randomized phase III trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT01803958) in 35 centers. Patients age ≥49 years with invasive breast cancer, resection margins ≥2 mm, tumor diameter ≤3 cm, and pN0-1 were randomly assigned 1:1 to WBI or APBI (38.5 Gy in 10 fractions twice daily). Neither patients nor investigators were masked to treatment allocation. The primary end point was ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR), analyzed according to the modified intention-to-treat analysis. We assumed a 5-year IBTR rate of 4% in the WBI group to exclude a 2% increase in the APBI group (90% power; noninferiority margin hazard ratio [HR], 1.5).
RESULTS: Between 2007 and 2019, 3,309 patients were randomly assigned (1,652 to APBI, 1,657 to WBI); 84 were excluded from the analysis. The median follow-up was 97.5 months. The 5-year cumulative IBTR incidence was 1.0% (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.6) for APBI and 0.8% (95% CI, 0.5 to 1.4) for WBI. The HR for APBI versus WBI was 1.18 (90% CI, 0.63 to 2.20) with the upper confidence limit crossing the prespecified noninferiority margin.
CONCLUSION: At 5 years, the cumulative incidence of IBTR is exceptionally low (≤1%) in both arms. Although formal statistical noninferiority was not demonstrated because the upper confidence limit crossed the margin, the absolute difference was <0.2%. External-beam APBI therefore is a reasonable clinical alternative to WBI for low-risk patients.
title: Partial-Breast Irradiation Versus Whole-Breast Irradiation for Low-Risk Invasive Breast Carcinoma: 5-Year Results of the Multicenter, Randomized, Phase III IRMA Trial.

 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) injection, the first treatment shown to help people with a severe form of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) live longer. Lembaz is approved to reduce the risk of death in adult and pediatric patients who weigh at least 7 kg (about 15 pounds) and whose neurological symptoms began before age 6, also known as infantile-onset NPC.
 “For families living with Niemann-Pick disease type C, today’s approval marks an important milestone,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “For the first time, there is a treatment shown to help adults and children with this serious disease live longer, and we are committed to continuing to support the development of therapies for the rare disease community.”
 Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder affecting an estimated 1 in 150,000 people, in which the body cannot properly process cholesterol and other fats inside cells. Over time, these substances accumulate — particularly in the brain — causing progressive neurological decline, including loss of movement, coordination, and the ability to swallow. Patients whose neurological symptoms begin before age 6 face the most serious form of the disease.
 Prior to this approval action, two therapies were approved for NPC, but neither has been shown to reduce the risk of death. Both carry age and weight restrictions that limit access for the youngest and most seriously affected patients. Lembaz is the first FDA-approved therapy to reduce the risk of death in adults and children weighing at least 7 kg (about 15 pounds) with NPC whose neurological symptoms began before age 6. A trained healthcare provider gives Lembaz as an injection directly into the spinal canal — a procedure called an intrathecal injection — every two weeks.
 To assess whether Lembaz reduced the risk of death, the FDA examined the survival of 36 patients treated with Lembaz across three clinical studies and an expanded access program. All patients had neurological manifestations of NPC that occurred prior to age 6. Patients treated with Lembaz had longer overall survival compared to the matched external control group, with a 55% reduction in the risk of death. The median survival time was 8.5 years for the treated group compared with 4.9 years in the control group. This survival benefit was observed regardless of whether patients were also taking miglustat, a therapy used off-label in NPC.
 The most common side effects of Lembaz include problems with hearing, balance and coordination, fatigue, vomiting, back pain, headache, fever, diarrhea, nausea, and cough. Lembaz carries a boxed warning for hearing impairment, including permanent hearing loss. A comprehensive hearing evaluation should be performed on patients before starting Lembaz and regularly throughout treatment, and dose adjustments may be needed based on the results of these evaluations.
 Lembaz received Breakthrough Therapy designation. The FDA granted approval of Lembaz to Mandos, LLC, a subsidiary of Beren Therapeutics, PBC.

text:
For Immediate Release: 
 November 17, 2026 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced the Global Reliance Disclosure Program (GRDP), a landmark initiative that will fundamentally transform how the FDA's regulatory drug and biologic approval decisions are leveraged by health authorities around the world. The GRDP marks a major step forward in the FDA's global leadership and may accelerate patient access to innovative therapies throughout the world.
 The GRDP enables the FDA to more efficiently share minimally redacted approval packages, including the FDA's detailed scientific and regulatory assessments, directly with companies who can then share them with regulatory authorities outside of the United States, empowering those authorities to rely on the FDA's rigorous, science-based review decisions rather than conducting duplicative and time-consuming product evaluations of their own, while maintaining sovereignty over their regulatory decision.
 "The GRDP is a prime example of America First policies improving public health worldwide," said Grace Graham, FDA Deputy Commissioner for Policy, Legislation, and International Affairs . "The FDA is the global gold standard and making it easier for applicants to leverage our detailed scientific assessments to facilitate faster access for patients everywhere is an example of America’s continued interest in advancing global health under the Trump Administration."
 The GRDP launched on Oct. 30, with a President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) tentative approval for lenacapavir , a drug indicated for both HIV prevention and treatment. This is an especially meaningful starting point given PEPFAR's life-saving mission to combat HIV/AIDS in some of the world's most vulnerable populations. The GRDP is currently available to PEPFAR tentative approvals, excluding tentatively approved abbreviated new drug application products. However, the FDA intends to expand the GRDP in January 2027 to all novel drug and biologics (New Molecular Entity New Drug Applications and 351(a) Biologics License Applications), dramatically broadening the program's reach and impact. 
 The FDA also intends to launch a pathway in early 2027 to expedite an applicant’s ability to request their minimally redacted action packages for approved and licensed drugs and biologics, accelerating global access to medicines that are already on the market in the United States and have been found to be safe and effective by the FDA.
 To receive a minimally redacted application approval package as part of the GRDP, applicants must request to participate within 10 calendar days of approval and confirm the application package is being submitted to a foreign regulatory authority in support of a marketing application. Applicants with eligible GRDP applications will receive detailed information in FDA approval letters and the agency intends to provide the minimally redacted package on an expedited basis. Requests for minimally redacted approval packages for other purposes will not be processed under the GRDP and should be submitted as a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request.
 “In an era of increasing global interdependence in pharmaceutical development and supply chains, the FDA's leadership is most effective when it is collaborative,” said Mark Abdoo, FDA Associate Commissioner for Global Policy and Strategy . “The GRDP reflects a forward-looking vision of regulatory leadership: one defined not by exclusivity, but by the willingness to share expertise, elevate global standards, and put patients first — wherever they are.” 
 The GRDP addresses one of the most persistent and consequential challenges in global health: the gap between regulatory approval in high-capacity countries and patient access in lower-resource settings. When a drug is approved by the FDA, patients in many parts of the world may wait months or years longer for their own national health authority to complete an independent review due to limited regulatory capacity and resources.
 Beyond individual product approvals, the GRDP supports global health security. Harmonized regulatory decisions reduce the risk of fragmented or inconsistent product standards across markets, helping to ensure that the same high-quality therapies reach patients regardless of where they live, including here in the United States.

Collaboration to support development of a stable, scalable formulation for clinical development and potential commercialization 
 SAN JOSE, Calif. , Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anixa Biosciences, Inc. ("Anixa" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: ANIX ), a biotechnology company focused on the treatment and prevention of cancer, today announced that it will work with Curia, a leading global contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO), to provide formulation development services for Anixa's investigational breast cancer vaccine in preparation for its upcoming Phase 2 clinical trial. The vaccine is being developed in collaboration with Cleveland Clinic.
 Under the collaboration, Curia will support the development of a formulation designed to optimize the vaccine's stability, consistency, and suitability for clinical manufacturing. This work represents an important step in Anixa's preparations for Phase 2 and is intended to establish a formulation and development process capable of supporting future clinical studies and potential commercial production.
 "Selection of Curia is another important milestone as we prepare to advance our breast cancer vaccine into Phase 2 clinical development," said Dr. Amit Kumar, Chairman and CEO of Anixa Biosciences. "Our Phase 1 trial demonstrated encouraging safety and immune-response results, and we are now focused on the activities necessary to support the next stage of clinical testing. Curia brings extensive expertise in pharmaceutical formulation and manufacturing processes, and we believe their capabilities will be valuable as we work toward developing a vaccine that could ultimately help prevent breast cancer."
 "Curia looks forward to providing formulation development support for Anixa's peptide cancer vaccine," said Ranald Baillie, VP, Drug Product Development and General Manager at Curia Glasgow. "Successful formulation and product development requires looking beyond the formulation itself to understand stability, analytical performance, scalability and the requirements of aseptic manufacturing. Curia's integrated expertise allows us to address those considerations early and develop robust processes designed to support Anixa as it advances this vaccine towards commercialization."
 Anixa's investigational breast cancer vaccine is designed to stimulate the immune system to recognize alpha-lactalbumin, a protein expressed in many breast cancers. The vaccine recently completed a Phase 1 clinical trial involving 35 women, meeting its primary endpoints and demonstrating a favorable safety and tolerability profile, with 74% of participants exhibiting protocol-defined immune responses. Anixa is preparing to advance the vaccine into Phase 2 clinical development to further evaluate its potential clinical benefits.
 About Curia 
Curia is a global contract development and manufacturing organization with more than 30 years of experience supporting pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies through drug discovery, development, and manufacturing. With an extensive global network of facilities, Curia provides integrated services spanning formulation development, analytical testing, process development, clinical manufacturing, and commercial production. Its Glasgow, Scotland facility specializes in sterile drug product development and manufacturing, including complex formulations, stability testing, lyophilization, and aseptic processing. For more information, visit www.curiaglobal.com .
 About Anixa Biosciences, Inc. 
Anixa is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on the treatment and prevention of cancer. Anixa's therapeutic portfolio consists of liraltagene autoleucel, or lira-cel, an ovarian cancer immunotherapy being developed in collaboration with Moffitt Cancer Center, which uses a novel type of CAR-T, known as chimeric endocrine receptor-T cell (CER-T) technology. This technology is differentiated from other cell therapies as the natural ligand of the FSHR receptor, FSH, binds to the FSHR receptor on the tumor cell instead of an antibody fragment. Moffitt is a world leader in cancer immunotherapy treatments, pioneering next-generation cell therapies such as CAR-T, and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to harness the power of the immune system. The Company's vaccine portfolio includes vaccines being developed in collaboration with Cleveland Clinic to treat and prevent breast cancer and ovarian cancer, as well as additional cancer vaccines to address many intractable cancers, including high incidence malignancies in lung, colon, and prostate. These vaccine technologies focus on immunizing against "retired" proteins that have been found to be expressed in certain forms of cancer. The breast and ovarian cancer vaccines were developed at Cleveland Clinic and exclusively licensed to Anixa. Cleveland Clinic is entitled to royalties and other commercialization revenues from the Company related to these vaccine technologies. Anixa's unique business model of partnering with world-renowned research institutions on all stages of development allows the Company to continually examine emerging technologies in complementary fields for further development and commercialization. The seventh symposium in Gangneung, South Korea, featured clinical research on REJURAN® polynucleotides and a behind-the-scenes look at how the products are made 
 GANGNEUNG, South Korea , Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PharmaResearch, the Korean pharmaceutical company behind the globally recognized skin booster REJURAN, brought together more than 750 medical professionals from 64 countries for its seventh PharmaResearch Global Symposium (PGS), held Oct. 26–28 in Gangneung, South Korea. The event gave clinicians working in aesthetic and regenerative medicine a chance to compare their experiences with polynucleotides (PN) and polydeoxyribonucleotides (PDRN) and discuss emerging approaches to treatment.
 Continue Reading
 The seventh PharmaResearch Global Symposium at the Gangneung Convention Center in Gangneung, South Korea. (Photo courtesy of PharmaResearch) 
 The program began with a look at how PharmaResearch sources and processes the raw material behind its PN and PDRN products. At a Korea Fisheries Resources Agency center, attendees saw how raw material is obtained from wild salmon and prepared for manufacturing. The tour continued at PharmaResearch's Gangneung plant, where they followed the material through processing, production and quality control.
 The scientific program turned to how REJURAN PN, developed using PharmaResearch's proprietary DNA Optimizing Technology (DOT ® ), is being studied and used in clinical practice. Across four sessions, clinicians discussed the evidence behind REJURAN, approaches to treatment and ways to improve the patient experience.
 Safety was one focus of the discussion. U.S. physician Dr. Suneel Chilukuri reviewed the safety profile of REJURAN PN, and Drs. Atchima Suwanchinda and Thanya Techapichetvanich from Thailand shared recent research on PN across several treatment areas. The program also examined what may be happening at the tissue level, with Australian physician Dr. Steven Liew discussing what histological findings suggest about how PN may support skin repair.
 Clinical cases brought those discussions into the treatment room. Dr. Yuri Yogya shared cases from his practice in Indonesia involving the lip area, while Japan's Dr. Soichiro Morikawa discussed his experience combining PN with other treatments.
 South Korean actress Kim Sejeong, a global ambassador for REJURAN and REJURAN COSMETICS, also attended the symposium.
 "It was an honor to be part of an event that brought together so many clinicians and researchers from around the world," Kim said. "I hope to bring REJURAN's message about caring for your natural beauty and feeling confident in yourself to more people around the world."
 "The symposium gave clinicians from around the world a chance to review the clinical evidence and safety data for DOT ® PN and discuss how that research could inform future treatment protocols," a PharmaResearch spokesperson said. "We'll continue to expand these exchanges in South Korea and internationally to help advance clinical practice in medical aesthetics."
 About PharmaResearch 
 PharmaResearch is a pioneering South Korean biopharmaceutical company dedicated to enhancing quality of life through regenerative medicine. Its portfolio spans medicines, medical devices, cosmetics and health supplements, built around its core DOT ® PDRN and DOT ® PN technologies, which are protected by multiple patents. PharmaResearch is headquartered in Gangneung, South Korea.
 The company is behind REJURAN, its globally recognized PN-based skin booster available in more than 50 countries, and REJURAN COSMETICS, its premium derma-cosmetic brand.
